ca_intersection_rock.blurb: Intersection Rock is the big roadside monolith beside Hidden Valley Campground in Joshua Tree National Park, and the most-climbed formation in the park. Its routes are mostly traditional crack and face lines on rough, grippy rock, from beginner-friendly cracks up through steady 5.10 and 5.11 testpieces. A few boulder problems and an aid line or two sit around the base. North Overhang is a popular 5.9, and Intersection Traverse is a well-known easy boulder circuit. Expect company on weekends, especially in cooler months, and plan on a standard trad rack. Slabs and chimneys turn slick when wet, so give the rock time to dry after rain.
ca_intersection_rock.parking_note: A parking area sits right behind the rock beside Hidden Valley Campground and takes cars and RVs. A vault toilet is next to it, and the trailhead for the Hidden Valley loop is close by.
ca_intersection_rock.approach: Only a few minutes on foot from the parking area; most routes start at the foot of the rock.

ca_picnic_area_boulders.blurb: The Picnic Area Boulders are a cluster of sandstone problems on Pine Mountain, high in the Los Padres mountains north of Ojai at roughly 7,000 feet. Nearly everything here is bouldering, with a big pile of easy and moderate problems in the V0 to V3 range, a solid group of V3 to V5 lines, and a few much harder ones. That mix, plus open flat landings and a shaded camp area close by, makes it a friendly place for newer boulderers and families. Popular problems include Painted Carnival, Morally Impaired and No Picnic. The elevation keeps it cooler than the coast, and the road in can be affected by winter snow, so check conditions before the long drive.
ca_picnic_area_boulders.parking_note: From Ojai take Highway 33 north about 30 miles to the Pine Mountain turnoff, then follow the paved, winding road roughly 6 miles to the camp area. The Picnic Area is the first campsite on your right. The road is narrow, so go slowly and honk before blind turns.

_expect.name: Pirate's Cove (aka The Beach or Corona Del Mar)

ca_pirate_s_cove_aka_the_beach_or_corona.blurb: Pirate's Cove is a small seaside bouldering spot below the cliffs at Corona del Mar in Newport Beach. The rock is sandstone: short caves and a low cliff, usually juggy but often damp and greasy from sea air. Almost all of the climbing is bouldering, from VB to V7 with most problems in the lower and middle grades, and soft sand landings that mean you sometimes can do without a big pad. Iron Man, Diamond Man and Paper Boy are among the standouts. Low tide gives you far more beach to work with, and late in the day the rock tends to be drier. Bring a brush and a towel for sandy shoes.
ca_pirate_s_cove_aka_the_beach_or_corona.parking_note: Drive to Corona del Mar State Beach, where you can park on Ocean Boulevard above the cove or in the lot down at the beach.
ca_pirate_s_cove_aka_the_beach_or_corona.approach: From the far west end of the beach parking lot, walk toward the harbor entrance, scramble over the rocks, and take the staircase down the cliff to the beach and boulders.

ca_aa_parkline_slab.blurb: Parkline Slab is a big south-facing slabby wall in the Lower Merced River Canyon, just inside Yosemite's western edge near El Portal and visible from Highway 140. Climbing is mostly traditional with some bolted sport lines, running from about 5.6 to the low 5.12s, and most routes sit between 5.8 and 5.11. Expect technical edging and smearing on slab to vertical rock, with longer multi-pitch lines on the wall. Hayley Anna and OtherWorld are popular. The sun hits the wall all day through winter, so it is a handy escape from cold days in the Valley. The rock can be loose and mossy in places, and the approach trail needs care so nothing is knocked onto the road below.
ca_aa_parkline_slab.parking_note: Park in the turnout below the cliff on the Highway 140 side, roughly a mile outside the Arch Rock entrance, on the El Portal side.
ca_aa_parkline_slab.approach: Start on the right side of the drainage and follow the faint climber's trail as it switchbacks up to the base of the slab. Do not scramble straight up the drainage, and avoid knocking rock onto the road.

ca_summit_area.blurb: The Summit Area is the high part of the Lake Ramona boulder field in northern San Diego County, on the hillside above the lake. Most of the climbing here is bouldering across a wide spread, V0 up to V9, with a smaller number of trad lines and top-ropes mixed in. Cracks, slabs and arêtes are all in play, and the trad and top-rope routes tend to be 5.10 and up. Ante Meridiem is a hard V7 problem, and Granite Geek and Slacker Cracker are the notable trad leads. Reaching the area takes a long, uphill walk in from the Blue Sky Ecological Reserve, so bring water and shade. The hike makes a nice morning outing even before you touch the rock.
ca_summit_area.parking_note: Leave the car at the Blue Sky Ecological Reserve lot; the walk to the Lake Ramona dam starts there.
ca_summit_area.approach: About 2.5 miles from the Blue Sky Ecological Reserve lot to the dam, with the last mile a steady uphill grind. The boulders sit on the hillside to the northwest of the lake.

ca_limbo_area.blurb: The Limbo Area is the middle of the three climbing zones in Mission Gorge, in Mission Trails Regional Park, with Middle Earth to the south and Main Wall to the north. It holds a mix of trad, sport and top-rope routes spread over several small walls, with plenty of moderates in the 5.7 to 5.9 range and the largest group at 5.10. Craig's Crack, a short hand crack, and Apostrophe are the trad highlights, and Madison is a good bolted line. The rock here is smooth and polished, so footwork matters more than you would expect for the grade. Some of the walls sit a fair way up the hillside. Arrive early, because the walls bake once the midday sun arrives.
ca_limbo_area.parking_note: From I-8 take the Mission Gorge/Fairmount exit and follow Mission Gorge Road into Mission Trails Regional Park. Park in the dirt lots by the visitor center, then walk to the climbers loop trails.
ca_limbo_area.approach: Start at the kiosk at the first climbers loop entrance, follow the trail up the hillside, then continue north. Some of the upper formations, Craig's Crack among them, take a bit more of a scramble up from Deviate Wall.

co_far_side.blurb: Far Side is one of the walls of The Gallery, the southernmost section of Shelf Road outside Canon City. It is almost all bolted limestone sport climbing, with a few trad lines, and the grades cluster in the 5.10 and 5.11 range with a good number of 5.8s and 5.9s as well. The limestone is steep and sustained, with crimps, pockets and flakes, and it can be a little brittle. Blackshirts, Flakeus Maximus and Well Hung are favorites. The wall is shaded in the afternoon, which helps on warm days, while the neighboring Mural Wall is the one that gets morning shade. Expect a 20 to 30 minute walk from the campground, and a 60 meter rope covers most routes here.
co_far_side.parking_note: Park at the Sand Gulch campground day-use area off Garden Park Road. A rough 4WD road reaches another lot nearer the wall, but most climbers walk in from Sand Gulch.
co_far_side.approach: From Sand Gulch take the trail through the campground and down into the wash, cross to the old Gallery parking area, head northwest, and take the left fork at the first junction to reach Far Side. Allow roughly 20 to 30 minutes.

co_rock_garden.blurb: The Rock Garden is a sport climbing area in the Penitente Canyon complex in the San Luis Valley, just behind the main canyon. The rock is volcanic welded tuff, hard and sharply featured, with a mix of small crimps, edges and pockets. Most of the climbing is bolted and runs from easy-moderate grades up through a large group of 5.11s and 5.12s, with a few 5.13s and some boulder problems and trad lines. The Reckoning, Do the Right Thing and DOA are well-known testpieces, and Ligneous Embracer is a standout easier line. Climbers here use colored chalk that blends with the rock. Some land nearby is private, so watch for and obey signs.
co_rock_garden.parking_note: From US 285 head west on County Road G for about six miles to La Garita, then follow County Road 38A and the signs to the Penitente turnoff.
